#4513. Ford Under Investigation for Airbags that Cause Burn Injuries

NHTSA has received several reports alleging burn injuries following airbag deployment in 2021–2026 Ford Explorers, with potentially 1.2 million units affected.

Ford is currently under investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation for more than a million vehicles whose front airbags could cause serious burns. According to the Preliminary Evaluation documents filed with the ODI, the investigation covers an estimated 1,236,155 Ford Explorer SUVs built between the 2021 and 2026 model years.

The investigation documents explain that the ODI has received eight Vehicle Owner Questionnaires and four Early Warning Reporting “Death and Injury” reports that include allegations of burn injuries caused by the deployment of the seat-mounted side airbags. Unfortunately, the filing suggests that the injuries have been fairly significant. The ODI documents show that the reported burn injuries associated with the investigation were typically diagnosed as second- or third-degree burns and required medical treatment to heal properly. According to the filing, some of the VOQs report injuries to law enforcement officers whose Police Interceptors’ side airbags were deployed.

The ODI’s preliminary evaluation will focus on determining the scope, frequency, and the safety ramifications caused by the defective airbags. #4512. Everyone wants an electric pickup truck. I want more electric 125cc motorcycles

If you follow the EV industry in North America, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the future of transportation revolves around electric SUVs and pickups. Every week seems to bring another teaser from a startup promising to reinvent the family car or truck. The latest electric SUVs, “coming soon” tiny trucks, lifestyle trucks, modular trucks, etc. Companies like Slate, TELO, and countless others have generated plenty of excitement, even if many of them still have everything left to prove.

Don’t get me wrong – I hope they succeed. We need more affordable electric vehicles. But after spending nearly two decades covering a specific part of the electric-vehicle space and a good chunk of that time traveling around the world to see how people actually get around, I can’t help but wonder if we’re chasing the wrong prize here.

Because while the West keeps trying to electrify pickup trucks and SUVs, much of the world has already settled on a far more sensible transportation appliance.

Western readers often think of a sedan as the world’s “normal” or “sensible” vehicle.

But go traveling almost anywhere in Asia, and that illusion disappears in about five minutes.

The roads are filled with Honda Clicks and CG125s, Hero Splendors, Yamaha NMAXs and YBR125s, and countless other small-displacement motorcycles. They carry workers to jobs, students to school, families to dinner, and every imaginable cargo in between.

They’re the delivery vans. They’re the commuter cars. They’re grocery getters, family transportation, and work trucks. And perhaps more importantly, they transport hundreds of millions of people every single day.

You don’t have to spend long in places like the Philippines before realizing something else: these aren’t really “motorcycle cultures.” They’re just transportation cultures. People ride these machines because they make sense.

And I’ve done it myself to see what all the fuss was about. Sure, I’m an e-motorcycle guy through and through. But I’ve been there to ride a mile in their motorcycle sandals, and so I get it.

Even so, having had one cheek on each saddle, I still have to think there’s a better way than the tried-and-true 125cc combustion engine motorcycles that have become the workhorse of much of the world.

The extreme proliferation of small motorcycles is what makes the current electric motorcycle market feel so strange. If there were ever a class of gasoline vehicle that batteries are already capable of replacing, it’s the 125cc combustion engine motorcycle.

These bikes aren’t demanding. They generally produce a modest 10-15 hp (8–11 kW) of power. They cruise comfortably around 45-60 mph (70-100 km/h). Most riders travel relatively short daily distances measured in dozens of miles, not hundreds.

A modern electric motorcycle with a 4-6 kWh battery can comfortably accomplish those same tasks while offering smoother acceleration, quieter operation, lower maintenance, and dramatically lower operating costs.

Unlike replacing a heavy-duty pickup truck that tows livestock trailers across Montana, replacing a 125cc commuter bike is already well within today’s battery technology. In many ways, it’s one of the easiest transportation sectors to electrify.

Instead, North America’s electric motorcycle market developed in an odd direction.

We have electric bicycles, and those are great for urban commuters. But then we jump almost straight to premium electric motorcycles costing $15,000 to $25,000. The practical middle has remained surprisingly sparse.

The ONYX RCR became something of a cult favorite by proving there was genuine demand for lightweight, motorcycle-like electric transportation without superbike performance.

Ryvid’s Anthem pushed further, adding highway capability while still remaining approachable and relatively affordable.

The new LiveWire S4 Honcho also feels like an encouraging step toward a lighter, more practical electric motorcycle instead of another oversized premium machine.

Even Infinite Machine’s Olto, while occupying a slightly different category, demonstrates growing interest in practical urban electric two-wheelers that prioritize transportation over headline horsepower.

These companies are proving something important: People don’t necessarily need 100 horsepower. Many simply need transportation.

Don’t misunderstand me. Electric pickup trucks absolutely have their place. Electric SUVs do too.

But we’ve spent the last decade pouring enormous engineering effort into electrifying some of the least energy-efficient passenger vehicles on the road.

Meanwhile, we’ve largely ignored one of the most efficient gasoline vehicle classes humanity has ever created.

A typical 125cc combustion engine motorcycle can already achieve fuel economy approaching or exceeding 100 mpg (2.35 liters/100 km). An electric equivalent becomes almost absurdly efficient.

We’re talking roughly 4-6 kWh per 100 kilometers (62 miles) – just a fraction of the energy consumed even by many compact electric cars. I once did the math, and a light electric motorcycle can travel 10,000 km (roughly 6,000 miles) for around $160 in electricity. Basically, your electrical bill doesn’t even notice when you own an electric motorcycle. Charging it simply doesn’t move the needle.

Instead of asking how we can fit ever-larger battery packs into increasingly larger SUVs and trucks, perhaps we should also be asking how many trips don’t need a large vehicle in the first place.

Transportation statistics across much of the developed world tell a familiar story.

Most trips involve one person. Maybe there’s also a backpack in the mix. Maybe there are some groceries getting picked up on the way home. Occasionally, there’s another passenger.

Those things are exactly what small motorcycles have been doing around the world for decades.

I recently spent some time in the Philippines, where I watched motorcycles carrying impossible-looking loads every day. Entire families would ride together. Construction materials. Furniture. Livestock. I saw two pigs on a 125cc bike, I kid you not. I’ve seen even crazier things in Thailand.

Again, I’m certainly not advocating that we adopt some of those practices in the West – there are obvious safety considerations – but it demonstrates just how incredibly capable these machines can be.

Even within normal Western expectations, a 125cc-class motorcycle is capable of handling an astonishing percentage of daily transportation needs.

This is where discussions about motorcycles often become unnecessarily polarized.

No, motorcycles aren’t ideal in every situation. Yes, heavy rain exists. Snow exists. Families with multiple children exist. Long interstate road trips exist.

Nobody is suggesting a 125cc electric motorcycle should replace every car.

If a household can replace even half of its daily driving with a lightweight electric motorcycle, that’s already a massive reduction in energy consumption, congestion, parking demand, and transportation costs.

Transportation doesn’t have to be all-or-nothing. So enough with this “but what if it rains?” stuff. Either put on a jacket that day or drive your car. But for the majority of the trips each year you take where it’s not raining, you could have done it in a much more efficient (and fun) way.

One of the biggest conversations surrounding EV adoption is charging. But smaller electric motorcycles barely participate in that problem. A 4-5 kWh battery charges overnight from an ordinary household outlet. The outlet you plug your laptop charger into is basically the equivalent of a Level 2 public charger for an e-motorcycle – that’s how fast it is.

DC fast charging isn’t really necessary on a light electric motorcycle. There’s no need for an expensive home charger. There’s no massive battery pack. Just plug it in before bed and wake up with a battery that’s been fully charged and waiting on you for hours already.

And if you want to go wild, there are swappable battery networks like Gogoro in Taiwan or Vammo in South America that can make charging unnecessary.

Another advantage rarely discussed is intimidation. Many people don’t want a 600 lb (270 kg) motorcycle producing superbike acceleration. They want something approachable, something lightweight, maneuverable, easy to park, and easy to live with.

That’s exactly why 125cc motorcycles became so successful globally.

Electric versions preserve all of those advantages while making them even easier to ride thanks to instant torque and the absence of clutch work. Many of them even come with reverse mode, making them easier to park and wiggle around even on hilly terrain.

One reason Europe has seen more progress here is that the regulatory framework already exists.

Manufacturers regularly market bikes as “125cc equivalents,” and consumers immediately understand what that means.

Licensing systems and insurance companies recognize the category. It’s a mature transportation class.

North America, by comparison, often treats motorcycles as either recreational toys or large-displacement touring machines. We’ve largely forgotten that much of the world simply sees them as transportation.

Ironically, younger riders may already be showing us the way forward.

The explosion in popularity of Sur Ron-style electric motorcycles and lightweight e-motos demonstrates that younger generations are perfectly willing to embrace two-wheeled electric transportation.

Not everyone buying those bikes is looking for motocross. Many simply enjoy the freedom, accessibility, affordability, and fun that come with traveling on two wheels.

Rather than dismissing that trend, perhaps we should recognize it as an opportunity. Today’s recreational rider often becomes tomorrow’s commuter.

If someone discovers they enjoy getting around on an electric two-wheeler, moving from a lightweight e-moto to a practical 125cc-equivalent commuter becomes a much smaller leap than convincing someone to abandon their car entirely.

One observation has stuck with me after so many years of covering the electric vehicle industry and traveling through countries where motorcycles dominate daily life. The West has spent years trying to electrify the largest, heaviest, and least efficient vehicles on our roads. Meanwhile, we’ve paid surprisingly little attention to electrifying the vehicle that already moves much of humanity every single day.

In Europe at least, there's a cliff between a pedal ebike, which anyone can ride without any pre planning, and a motorcycle which needs passing a specific test, taxing, taking out insurance and wearing safety gear. Even people with car licences need to take driving lessons and the test. It means you can't just step on a motorcycle when it makes sense you need potentially months of planning. It's much easier just to take a car you're already licensed for.

I’m not arguing that everyone should ride a motorcycle. And I’m certainly not arguing that cars no longer have an important place.

But perhaps we’ve underestimated just how many people could benefit from something in between.

Not just an electric bicycle, and not just a $25,000 electric motorcycle. Just an honest, practical, affordable electric equivalent of the vehicle that already keeps much of the world moving.

Because if we’re serious about accelerating electric transportation, maybe the future isn’t another electric pickup truck. Maybe it’s finally giving the world’s favorite motorcycle an electric motor.

#4511. College student develops LEGO-like, 3D-printed moon bricks

Published Nov 10, 2026 4:30 PM EST

A permanent lunar base will require structures resilient enough to withstand everything from cosmic radiation and micro-meteorites to moonquakes. There are plenty of building materials to choose from on Earth, but they all come with a catch: transportation storage aboard spacecraft is limited, and each additional pound of cargo will quickly ramp up costs. Engineers have spent years experimenting with ways for future astronauts to source local lunar ingredients, including fine moon dust known as regolith. Unfortunately, most require various binding ingredients that must still be sent from back home.

A college student at the University of Arkansas (U of A) recently had a different idea. In a collaboration with U of A mechanical engineer Wan Shou, Cole McCallum harnessed a specialized method of 3D printing to manufacture LEGO-esque bricks from lunar dust, no binding required. (These aren’t to be confused with LEGO’s actual lunar bricks mockups). Their results published in the journal NPJ Advanced Manufacturing indicate the bricks could be a promising material to investigate as humanity readies itself for a return to the moon.

Lunar regolith is a tricky material. Unlike Earth’s dirt, it doesn’t contain any amount of organic matter. It’s just loose, sharp-edged particles generated by billions’ of years of asteroid and meteor impacts. This means that moon dust can’t bind on its own and requires at least some secondary ingredients.

While an undergraduate at the U of A, McCallum wondered if a specific type of 3D printing called laser powder bed fusion could offer a workaround. In this technique, fine powder is placed on a flat bed, then exposed to a highly powerful laser beam that fuses each microscopic particle together in a process called sintering. The tray bed lowers down to allow another layer of sintered powder, then repeats the steps until a single, solid block is created. Regolith fits the mold perfectly, so to speak.

“There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum said in a university profile.

McCallum and Shou didn’t have access to actual lunar material, so they obtained Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercial material that replicates the moon dust collected by Apollo astronauts during the 1960s and 70s. They ultimately settled on two shapes, one that resembles a cross and another that looks like the letter “H.” The researchers then 3D-printed tiny prototypes measuring a few centimeters wide that they could connect like LEGOs to construct larger structures.

There are still some important caveats to this sintered regolith strategy. McCallum’s blocks are much more porous and weaker than materials containing binders. Additional research is needed to see how the approach works in a vacuum or microgravity, two inescapable hurdles to living on the moon.

“These structures we’re making can be self-supported. But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet,” said McCallum.

That said, his demonstration that even a basic framework for lunar base bricks is achievable solely with regolith may offer a promising direction for mission engineers

#4510. Gift Guide: Best Tech and Gadgets for Gearheads and Car Lovers

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Keep up with the latest automotive and garage tech with our picks for the best gadgets and tech on the market today.

This article was updated in November 2026.

Automotive enthusiasm has always gone hand in hand with a fascination for technology. At Road & Track, we’re always interested in the technology that makes the automotive experience better.

Some are practical necessities, others are just plain cool, but each has something to offer a car enthusiast. Think diagnostic scanners, GPS navigation systems, performance monitors, wireless phone accessories, and clever tools that help tackle jobs around the garage.

We’ve included options at various price points and for different kinds of enthusiasts, so you can find something useful, interesting, and worth keeping in the toolbox.

The Mission 1 Pro is built for capturing the kind of driving footage that makes you want to take the long way home. I recently used one myself on a drive up the Pacific Coast Highway, where its compact size made it easy to bring along and its high-resolution video captured everything from sweeping coastal views to the little details along the road. It’s a versatile action camera for car enthusiasts who want more than a few phone clips from their next road trip, with the rugged, portable design GoPro has built its reputation on.

The Cobra RAD 700i is less a radar detector and more a digital co-pilot for the fast lane. With long-range detection, GPS-powered AutoLearn filtering, and Bluetooth connectivity to Cobra’s Drive Smarter network, it helps cut through false alerts while keeping you tuned into live speed traps, cameras, and roadside hazards. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility sweeten the deal, turning your windshield into mission control for highway miles and heavy right feet.

A navigation app is only as useful as the cellular connection behind it, and that can become a problem once you get far enough outside town. The weBoost Drive X is a multi-user cellular signal booster that uses an external magnetic-mount antenna to capture available signals, then amplifies them for devices inside the cabin. Its amplifier delivers up to 50 dB of gain and supports several major U.S. cellular frequency bands. The kit includes both exterior and interior antennas, a power supply, and the amplifier itself, making it a worthwhile consideration for road trippers, overlanders, and anyone who regularly ventures beyond reliable cell coverage.

Running navigation, streaming music, and charging wirelessly can turn a smartphone into a little pocket-size space heater, especially on a summer road trip. Pioneer’s SDA-SC600 combines a magnetic Qi2 charging mount with an integrated cooling fan designed to help manage device temperatures during longer drives. It supports wireless charging at up to 15 watts, includes an adjustable air-vent mount, and uses a multicolor LED indicator to show charging status.

A phone running Google Maps isn’t going to cut it when the pavement ends and the trail network gets complicated. The Garmin Tread 2 Overland Edition is an eight-inch, glove-friendly GPS navigator built specifically for off-road travel, with preloaded topographic maps of North and South America, public-land information, and U.S. Forest Service Motor Vehicle Use Maps. Its IP67-rated enclosure is designed to withstand dust, water exposure, and rough conditions, while the included magnetic-assisted locking mount secures the unit to the dashboard. It also supports downloadable satellite imagery and route planning through Garmin’s Tread app, giving overlanders a much more capable navigation setup than a smartphone alone.

If you're serious about reverse-engineering custom car parts or replicating impossible-to-find trim pieces, a high-quality 3D scanner is a garage game-changer. The Creality Sermoon P1 takes the clunky laptop out of the equation by packing an advanced blue-laser and NIR structured-light scanner into a standalone, tetherless device. With a built-in 6-inch touchscreen and powerful onboard processing, you can scan, mesh, and export digital models of engine bays or body panels directly from the unit without tripping over cables. It delivers metrology-grade 0.02mm accuracy, features a single-line laser mode to effortlessly capture deep holes and bolt recesses, and handles shiny metal or dark automotive plastics without requiring messy matte spray.

The BlueDriver Bluetooth Pro OBD2 Scanner is a compact diagnostic tool that plugs into a vehicle’s OBD-II port and sends information wirelessly to an iOS or Android device. Beyond reading and clearing standard check-engine codes, it offers enhanced diagnostics for systems such as ABS, airbags, transmission, and TPMS on supported vehicles. The companion app also provides live sensor data, Mode 6 test results, and repair reports with possible causes and reported fixes. With compatibility covering most 1996-and-newer North American vehicles and no subscription fees, it’s a useful step up from a basic code reader for anyone who likes doing their own troubleshooting.

A stopwatch can tell you whether your last lap was faster, but it won’t explain why. The Garmin Catalyst is a dedicated track-driving analysis system that combines a 10Hz multi-GNSS receiver, onboard accelerometers and gyroscopes, and an HD remote camera to record and evaluate a driver’s performance. Garmin’s True Track Positioning technology analyzes racing lines, braking points, apexes, and track-out positions, while its True Optimal Lap feature combines the best sections of recorded laps to show how much time is potentially left on the table. It can also deliver real-time audio coaching, making it a particularly interesting tool for track-day drivers who want to improve without investing in a complicated professional data-logging setup.

DJI’s Mini 4 Pro is packed full of impressive imaging capabilities and innovative navigation features. The 249-gram weight of the unit means the device is just under the Federal Aviation Administration’s 250-gram limit for registering your drone in the United States, significantly reducing the barriers to entry other drones require. The Mini 4 Pro captures 4K video at up to 100 frames per second (fps) or 4K at 60 fps with HDR video. The unit is rated for roughly 12 miles of transmission between the drone and the included remote, ensuring even congested areas or valleys/hills won’t impact your ability to record video or snap photos. Other features include 360-degree obstacle-avoidance sensors, a plethora of automated capture modes capable of locking in on and tracking subjects, and a 34-minute flight time with the included batteries.

Stop stuffing your pockets with multiple flashlights when you really just need this one. Holding the ArkPro Ultra feels immediately different than a standard flashlight; the flat, slim profile disappears in your pocket or EDC bag unlike bulky round tubes, yet the unibody aluminum feels incredibly dense and premium in the hand. It solves the biggest headache of carrying high-tech gear: charging anxiety. Because it finally supports both magnetic snap-charging and standard USB-C, you can top it off on your nightstand or with a laptop cable without hunting for a proprietary cord. Whether you are running a presentation or checking for leaks under a car, it feels like the Swiss Army knife of light that actually performs as well as the dedicated tools it replaces.

The IntelliDash Pro X10 is a modern shortcut for aging dashboards—a slim 10-inch touchscreen that brings wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto to just about any car without surgery, swearing, or a weekend in the garage. Setup is gloriously plug-and-play, with Bluetooth, FM, AUX, and voice-assistant support baked in. Big maps, brighter road trips, cleaner cable chaos. It’s the kind of upgrade that makes a 2009 commuter vehicle feel a little more spaceship.

A shiny new paint job can hide a lot of history, particularly on an older car that’s been through a few owners and at least one body shop. The Rdinscos Car Coating Thickness Meter is designed to measure the thickness of paint and other coatings on metal panels, giving buyers a way to compare readings across a vehicle’s bodywork. Uneven measurements can point toward previous refinishing, additional layers of paint, or body filler, making the tool particularly useful when inspecting a potential project or evaluating a used-car purchase. It’s not a replacement for a trained eye or a proper pre-purchase inspection, but it can help uncover evidence of repairs that a quick walkaround might miss.

The Hoto Tools Precision Screwdriver Kit Pro is a wonderful gift for any DIY aficionado or professional. The screwdriver uses a two-gear design to provide more than enough torque for delicate builds or repairs. It also features built-in LED lights and an innovative contact charging case that stores the drill and its accessories, ensuring power is always topped off when needed.

This kit isn’t just about looks—it’s about substance, with 48 bits forged from S2 steel, complemented by a suite of practical tools like spudgers, tweezers, and a suction cup for those tricky parts. The electric screwdriver’s adjustable torque and handy magnetizer/demagnetizer tool help to ensure no small bits and pieces go missing. Whether you’re a tech enthusiast or a creative tinkerer, the Hoto Tools kit provides practicality and precision in a compact, stylish package.

Built for gloveboxes, road trips, and “oh no” moments, the Vantrue JS3 is a compact four-in-one roadside powerhouse: jump starter, air compressor, fast-charging power bank, and emergency light, in one rugged shell. With a 3250-amp peak current, 160-psi inflator, and USB-C PD 65-watt charging, it’s designed to revive dead batteries, refill tires fast, and keep devices alive when the highway gets unpredictable. Think of it as roadside insurance with a lithium heartbeat.

Shopping for someone who already has every gadget is tough, but the Insta360 X6 is a guaranteed win. Because it shoots in every direction at once, you don’t even have to worry about framing—just hit record and pick the best angles later on your phone. The software automatically edits out the selfie stick, making it look like a low-flying drone is following you, whether you’re carving up back roads, hitting the mountain bike trails, or just messing around in the backyard. It’s incredibly easy to use and makes literally any activity look epic.

Reverse-engineering a custom intake manifold or replicating a classic car’s unobtainium trim pieces usually means dragging a fragile laptop into the grime of the garage. The Creality Sermoon P1 standalone 3-D scanner finally severs that tether. This isn’t some plastic hobbyist toy; it’s a high-octane engineering workstation crammed into a handheld chassis. Packing a Qualcomm 8-core processor and a massive 24GB of RAM, the P1 processes dense 3-D meshes directly on its crisp six-inch touchscreen. It boasts enough onboard horsepower to digitize a complete engine block without breaking a single drop of digital sweat. For the uncompromising gearhead looking to turn physical metal into flawless digital data, the Sermoon P1 is the ultimate garage weapon.

This cordless four-in-one Slim V8 Apex mini vacuum packs 19,000Pa suction into a glovebox-friendly frame, with attachments for crumbs, cupholders, keyboards, pet hair, and other chaos agents. It also blows, inflates, and pumps, making it equal parts detail tool and travel sidekick. Lightweight, USB-C rechargeable, and surprisingly mighty, it’s built for people who treat messes like pit stops—not permanent conditions.

The Nextmug Go is the kind of gadget that quietly upgrades your entire morning ritual. This sleek, self-heating travel mug keeps coffee or tea at your preferred temperature — Warm, Hot, or Piping — for hours, so every sip tastes freshly poured. Its spill-resistant lid, long-lasting battery, and app-free controls make it refreshingly simple to use on commutes, road trips, or marathon workdays. Think of it as a thermos with a master’s degree in modern convenience.

HoverAir’s X1 ProMax is the ultimate drone for people who don’t know anything about drones. This self-flying, fully enclosed camera launches from your hand and uses 10+ AI-powered shooting and follow modes to capture photographs and up to 8K/30 (or 4K/120) video, stabilized by SmoothCapture 2.0—a two-axis gimbal with electronic image stabilization (EIS) and horizon leveling. It’ll track confidently with a rated 42 km/h (26 mph) follow speed, and its OmniTerrain feature is designed for flying near water, snow, and other tricky surfaces. I’ve shot various drones over the years, and while others might be more technically capable, none are as simple to use as the ProMax. The best part is, it’ll fit nearly anywhere. It’s a no-brainer for anyone who wants to capture drone footage quickly in a device that folds up smaller than most books.

Ride1Up’s Revv 1 DRT is a moped-style e-bike that trades Lycra vibes for dirt-track energy. A 52-volt system feeds a 1000-watt Bafang rear hub and a 35-amp controller with a “boost” party trick, while a 52-vole/20-Ah UL-certified pack (about 1040 watt-hours) keeps the lights on. Off-road mode unlocks 28-plus mph for private property, and the chassis gets real hardware: a 150-mm dual-crown fork, 76 mm of rear travel, and flur-piston hydraulic stoppers. Range is quoted at 30–60 miles, and the whole package carries UL 2849/2271 safety certifications—welcome peace of mind on a 30-mph pseudo-moto.

On trail or torn-up alleys, the DRT feels like a small, electric pit bike: confident, quick to squirt, and more fun than it has any right to be. The flip side is familiar: short cranks and moped geometry make real pedaling an afterthought, knobby 20-by-fours hum and nibble at range, and you’ll want to mind local laws before touching that off-road setting. At $2395, it undercuts many fashion-forward rivals while delivering genuine off-road chops and useful kit (headlight fairing, molle mounting, twist throttle). If your commute occasionally turns to dirt, this is the hooligan commuter to beat.

#4509. Audi Has Officially Ended Production of the A8 Flagship Sedan

After more than thirty years, Audi presses pause on its biggest sedan.

Ever since Skipp Sudduth asked for “Something very Fast. Audi S8. Something that can shove a little bit,” in 1998's Ronin, Audi's big body sedan has been the stuff of legend. Mercedes-Benz S-Class? Too obvious. BMW 7-Series? You don't want to look like a wannabe James Bond. But an Audi A8? That's what you drive when you have a nickname like The Transporter.

However, as appealing as the A8 is on-screen, it's not really been much of a mover in Audi showrooms of late. Almost nothing depreciates faster than a full-size German luxury sedan—you might as well invest in an ice sculpture—and both BMW and Mercedes have been outselling Audi in the segment. Thus, Audi has just pressed pause on production of the A8, with no immediate plans in place to reboot it.

See all results for new 2027 Audi A8 for sale near 63129

The Neckarsulm plant where the A8 was being built has already pivoted to production of the Audi A5 in both sedan and Avant forms, in standard and S5 or RS5 trims. Audi has been headquartered in Ingolstadt since the 1980s, long enough to have that city be shorthand for the company the way Stuttgart is for Porsche, but the Neckarsulm plant has roots stretching back to the nineteenth century via NSU, one of the companies that ended up forming Audi's four rings

Launched in 1994, the A8 arrived with aluminum-intensive construction to keep weight down and an available 4.2-liter V8 that still rates as one of the best-sounding engines ever made. It was businesslike, composed with all-wheel-drive for all conditions, managing to be both discreet and muscular, like a bodyguard in a well-tailored suit.

Subsequent generations remained a little more understated than rivals from Mercedes and BMW, but the fifth-gen car that's just exited production was only a year away from celebrating its tenth birthday. Even with a mid-cycle facelift, that's a bit long in the tooth for a flagship.

Taking over flagship duties is Audi's Q9 SUV, a proper three-row family hauler that's aimed at the BMW X7 and Mercedes GLS. The Q9 is certainly large and imposing, and it can carry more passengers and cargo than any A8 model. Does it have that same charisma? Put it this way: Jason Bateman is a very talented actor and producer. He is not Jason Statham.

Meanwhile, Audi may return with some kind of electrified successor to the A8, perhaps as an extended, embiggened version of whatever the new battery-electric A4 ends up looking like. Until then, any Audi-loving underworld soldiers of fortune will have to make do with a brown Mercedes 450 SEL 6.9 and a rocket launcher.

#4508. New ID. AURA is the mainstream EV VW needs – but its software is the real story

Volkswagen built its global empire on the promise of affordable, accessible transportation, embodied by the iconic Type 1 Beetle. Now facing an existential crisis after a decades-long push upmarket, the automaker faces a reckoning – and a retreat back into affordable, mass-market electric sedans like the new FAW-VW ID. AURA L5 (and the software that powers it) might be exactly what VW needs to reach a new generation of buyers.

Like the Ford Model T, the original VW Type 1 Beetle was an engineering-led answer to a basic problem: making family transportation affordable and accessible to the masses. And regardless of how you feel about Elon Musk, the Tesla Model 3 has become the spiritual successor to those cars, bringing electric transportation to millions of mainstream drivers. As the Model 3 approaches its 11th year in public view, the recently revealed all-electric ID. AURA L5 and VW JETTA looks like it could be a compelling rival to the mainstream M3.

Co-developed by Volkswagen’s Chinese and German design teams and set to be built by the FAW-VW JV, the ID. AURA L5 is an Accord/Camry-sized electric family car a practical fastback-style rear hatch, frameless doors, and a claimed “84.4% usable floor-area ratio.” The power-operated hatchback opens its maw more than 70 degrees, revealing a 39″ wide opening that can handle groceries, luggage, golf clubs, pets, bodies – whatever you got.

Don’t take my word for it, though. This is the original text from the company’s press release (translated from Chinese by Google):

The ID. AURA L5 is a pure electric family sedan, jointly designed by Chinese and German design teams, and highly replicates the design essence of the ID. AURA concept car shown at the 2025 Shanghai Auto Show. Its short overhang and long wheelbase proportions create a sleek and flowing coupe-like stance, achieving a “usable floor area ratio” of 84.4%. The sides feature true frameless doors, semi-concealed door handles, and an electric hatchback tailgate with an opening angle exceeding 70°, and an opening width exceeding 1000 mm, greatly improving the convenience of loading and unloading large items, deeply integrating fastback aesthetics with practicality. Some models will be equipped with LiDAR and feature the Hyper Sense 8 end-to-end large model, making daily travel easier and more convenient for customers.

The production version of the ID. AURA L5 is expected to pack the same 155 kW (~208 hp) electric motors announced when the concept AURA L5 was first shown last year (battery specs were not released), and was shown as part of a broader product announcement of what VW Group China would be showcasing at this year’s China International Import Expo (CIIE). These include the first two models fully equipped with Volkswagen Group’s locally developed VEGA “integrated technology matrix” (read: software), and the Volkswagen Anhui intelligent pure electric “coupe” crossover.

The announcement coincides with reports from outlets like Autocar and Reuters that Volkswagen is evaluating whether to deploy its China-developed electrical architecture across the majority of its European markets.

“According to internal discussions confirmed by Group board member and Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer,” reports Autocar’s Greg Kable, “up to 75% of the firm’s core models in Europe could eventually use the China Electronic Architecture.”

The Volkswagen Group has been struggling to deliver a software experience that resonates with customers. To their credit, they’re looking for outside help, spending billions of dollars on a software collaboration with EV startup Rivian for its upcoming electric truck brand Scout rather than going it alone. With billions of dollars and potential future of the company at stake, then, this seems like the most interesting bit of the announcement:

During the event, the immersive interactive experience exhibit “Digital Magic Cube,” which made its debut at last year’s China International Import Expo, will undergo an iterative upgrade to showcase the core strength of CEA (China Electronic Architecture), the software pillar of Volkswagen Group’s integrated self-developed technology matrix VEGA, to the attendees.

To date, CEA has enabled five new models from three joint ventures within the Volkswagen Group on a large scale, and software iterations have already been completed this year. CEA brings three core advantages to the Group’s new model lineup in China: intelligent accessibility, continuous upgrades, and safety redundancy. Through immersive interactive presentations, it provides consumers with the most intuitive experience. Empowered by the new AI R&D toolchain “C-Brain,” CEA introduces AI agents into software development, design, and engineering verification, enabling more flexible and efficient integration and innovation of vehicle intelligence capabilities, giving vehicles powerful thinking and perception abilities. Intelligent vehicles powered by CEA can better understand consumer needs, more efficiently create in-vehicle intelligent application scenarios, and better enhance digital intelligent safety redundancy, bringing Chinese consumers a new generation of intelligent mobility experience defined by Volkswagen standards

Sensible looking average car which should appeal to VW buyers provided the price, charging speed and range are right. Especially like that it has a hatch without being SUV shaped.

The show runs through November 10th, and we’ll be keeping an eye out for more details on the ID. AURA lineup and the Anhui intelligent pure electric coupe, including its powertrain, battery, and software specifications, as they become available.

#4507. ‘One-in-a-million’ yellow fish found in New York

Published Nov 11, 2026 8:22 AM EST

We’ll call him mellow yellow. An  “exceptionally rare” yellow-colored burbot (Lota lota) was recently caught by a team of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) biologists in Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario in Upstate New York.

Burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia. To the naked eye, they appear scaleless, but are actually covered with tiny, almost microscopic scales. What they eat depends on their size. Smaller burbots will eat zooplankton, while bigger burbots prefer to snack on other fish.

The team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey. It gets its unique color from a rare genetic condition called xanthochromism. A genetic mutation suppresses the normal pigmentation, and produces a yellow-orange appearance instead of the burbot’s usual grey, olive, or tan coloring. In wild fish, xanthochromism is less common than albinism or melanism, making this fish an “especially unusual capture.”

The burbot is a native species in the Great Lakes, but the USFWS team says the discovery highlights the effectiveness of the Service’s Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program. The program uses a multi-gear fish-surveillance strategy to detect certain non-native species in the harbors, rivers, and embayments of the Great Lakes. Early detection of a watchlist species gives fisheries managers the best opportunity to implement prevention and removal measures if invasive species are detected. Since invasive species are often rare when they first enter new waters, the program uses electrofishing, fyke-netting, gill-netting, and environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis to increase the chances that scientists detect an invasive species.

“The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor,” the USFWS wrote in a statement. “It represents the first documented detection of a burbot during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few angler catches have been reported.”

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) fisheries biologists, who examined the fish and are familiar with the species, also observed that it was very thin and appeared to be in poor health. It was later sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis due to the “unexplained factors contributing to the continued suppression of its population”

“The discovery could turn out to be lucky for the burbot too; this exceptionally rare fish may provide valuable insight into the health of the species’ populations throughout the basin that can inform management actions,” the USFWS concluded.

#4506. 10,000 Miles with Our 2026 Mercedes-Benz E450, and the Love Bombing Continues

We can’t get enough of the way the E-class drives.

If you were friends with our long-term Mercedes-Benz E450, and it was in a relationship with someone like us, you’d be no doubt cautioning your friend about our love bombing. The logbook is stuffed, page after page, with over-the-top praise. Here’s a smattering of some recent musings: “Arguably the most comfortable long-termer we’ve ever had,” says managing news editor Eric Stafford. Senior news editor Caleb Miller added, “The E450 just feels so effortless and relaxing that I feel like I could drive across the country in one day in this thing.” And Miller also gave a shoutout to the 21-speaker Burmester sound system. Editor-in-chief Tony Quiroga, who is known to sign out the E-class for extended chunks of time, adds, “Makes you feel so relaxed when you drive it—supple ride, glorious seats, rich interior, plus summer-tire grip.” But Buyer’s Guide director Rich Ceppos may have bestowed the highest praise: “Of the 500-plus models we cover, if I had to pick one car to live with and drive every day, it’d be this one.”

See all results for new 2026 Mercedes-Benz E-class for sale near 21014

It’s safe to say we’re smitten with the way the E-class drives, an ideal blend of comfort and liveliness. If we had one nit to pick it would be the slight impact harshness from the 20-inch wheels and tires and their relatively shallow sidewalls. We’d probably like the ride better with the base 18-inch wheel-and-tire package and its additional sidewall, although it’s a major visual downgrade.

The E450 drives so well, and its 375-hp turbo inline-six is so smooth and melodious, that we’d be more than willing to overlook so-so fuel economy. But the E-class continues to impress there, too, with an overall average of 27 mpg, one better than its EPA combined figure. And that’s with a lot of heavy-footed commuting and not all that many road trips. On longer drives, we’ve seen mpg numbers in the high 30s.

Fall’s cooler temperatures have us in a warm glow about the E450’s not only heated steering wheel and seats (both pretty common nowadays) but also the heated center and outboard armrests, part of the $2950 Multicontour Seating package—decadent, perhaps, but a lovely way to start your commute on a chilly morning.

Our primary complaints tend to be about anything but the driving, including the touch-sensitive controls on the steering wheel, the door handles that sometimes don’t power out of the body quick enough, or the fingerprint-prone piano-black interior trim and vast array of three screens across the interior. We’ve also gotten plenty cross with the virtual assistant, which chimes in with obnoxious frequency if left to its automatic setting, interrupting conversations about everything from building developments in the area to the price of an item discussed. We quickly switched it back to having to hear the “Hey, Mercedes” wake phrase before inserting itself.

See all results for new 2026 Mercedes-Benz E-class for sale near 21014

You know the honeymoon phase is waning when it comes time to start paying for maintenance. Mercedes specifies service for the E-class every 10,000 miles or 12 months, with the first one a simple oil change and various inspections. We felt the Mercedes markup paying that $478 bill, and our local dealer added another $62 of oil and fuel additives that aren’t called for in the owner’s manual and without asking our approval (we’ve excluded this charge from the service-cost tally).

The only other pause in the enjoyment of our E450 was when a screw found its way into the right-front tire in a spot where it couldn’t be plugged. So, we had to shell out $420 for a new tire from Tire Rack, which was there the next day.

Can the love last? We have another 30,000 miles to find out.

Months in Fleet: 5 months Current Mileage: 11,134 milesAverage Fuel Economy: 27 mpgFuel Tank Size: 17.4 gal Observed Fuel Range: 460 milesService: $478 Normal Wear: $0 Repair: $0Damage and Destruction: $420

Ever since this long-term 2026 Mercedes-Benz E450 arrived, it has served us daily reminders why we named this excellent luxury sedan to our 10Best list for two years running. Some of that luxury comes from the fact that we could not drive the car in any other way, because it showed up with a mere 20 miles on its odometer and we were driving gently to follow the 1000-mile break-in requirements. Either way, its ride refinement and all-around sophistication have received continuous accolades since day one. Everyone in the office is already gushing over the E-class's ride quality, refinement, and seat comfort.

Of course, once we hit the 1000-mile mark, we picked up the pace. The around-town ride feels almost floaty, so you'd think that hurling it down a back road would take the E450 out of its element, but it remains tied down and settled no matter how hard you push. Skidpad grip of 0.92 g is excellent for the class, as is braking from 70 mph in 157 feet, which is an identical result to the last BMW M5 we tested.

The E450's inline-six, which pairs exclusively with all-wheel drive and is a $5900 upgrade over the four-cylinder-powered E350, is not only smooth and sonorous, but also extraordinarily fuel efficient. We measured a whopping 39 mpg in our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, which is 6 mpg better than its EPA highway figure. Combined with a decently sized 17.4-gallon fuel tank, that means our E-class can make it nearly 700 miles on a single fill-up. The E450 returns excellent fuel economy beyond purposefully gentle driving too; our current running average of 27 mpg is 1 mpg higher than its EPA combined rating. Considering the straight-line hustle the 375-hp six commands—60 mph in a brisk 4.5 seconds and the quarter-mile in 12.9 seconds—that fuel economy is seriously impressive.

But the steering wheel's touch-sensitive controls are despised as much as the car's overall driving demeanor is loved. Everything from the volume control to the cruise set speed requires a swipe on the steering-wheel spokes, which sometimes does nothing, sometimes provides more adjustment than you're looking for, and rarely does exactly what you want.

Our long-term E450 is packed full of options, taking the price up to $95,375 from its $73,650 starting point. There are a few things that the majority of us could do without, including the front passenger screen and selfie camera (part of the $1500 Superscreen package) and the $990 3-D gauge cluster display. But the $3400 Pinnacle trim, which includes a thumpin' 21-speaker Burmester stereo, and the $3200 air springs that bolster ride quality are outlays that we'd spend our own money on. We also thought ahead to winter; tucked into the various option packages are heaters for the front armrests, steering wheel, rear seats, and washer nozzles. There's really only one feature that we wish we had, and that's soft-close doors, which cost an additional $550. We're fans of the Verde Silver Metallic green paint, and the $1950 20-inch AMG multi-spoke wheels are a serious visual upgrade over the base 18s.

The E-class is not at all ostentatious, but it still gets noticed, with many a parking-lot bystander lobbing praise in the E-class's direction. We agree, it's a fantastic luxury sedan, and we look forward to spending a lot more time driving it to see if we're as smitten with the ownership experience.

#4505. French carmaker Renault wants to get into the military robot business

Forget what your Fox News-addicted uncle told you about cheese-eating surrender monkeys. The French military has centuries of storied military victories and traditions behind it, and Renault wants in on that action with a new, autonomous electric vehicle platform designed to tackle the Armée de Terre’s most demanding missions.

Co-developed by the EV experts at Renault Group and the defense experts at Belgian electronics firm John Cockerill, the new Forefront concept previews a new, modular ground vehicle that can be rapidly industrialized at a controlled cost, with unique mobility and off-road performance, and capable of autonomously navigating complex terrain. The result is a machine that could front-line logistical capabilities for both defense and civilian applications, enabling missions to be carried out remotely in very high-risk and hard‑to‑reach environments.

“Forefront Concept … demonstrates the contribution that Renault Group’s industrial and technological expertise can make to a strategic sector such as unmanned ground vehicles with multiple applications expected across both civilian and military sectors in the years to come,” explains François Provost, CEO, Renault Group. “This innovative project brings together two complementary areas of expertise: Renault Group’s in the rapid, large-scale and cost-effective development and production of high-performance, reliable technological products and John Cockerill’s in the defense industry.”

Renault is quick to point out that its new concept isn’t just suitable for military work. Although it’s worth pointing out that the Renault-provided image, above, isn’t just AI slop: it would be impractical if it was real, with no real obvious way to get those RCP pipes on or off the thing. That said, presenting their military killbot as a construction mule is at least more credible than the “ambulance” and “troop transport” use cases we’ve seen touted by similar concepts on the American side.

Call me cynical but military contracts are the best and last refuge for a company that cannot compete in the open market. With no / limited international competition, a famously slow procurement process that favors "proven" (read 3+ generation old) technology, and equipment that is rarely used in a competitive environment and whose failures are cloaked behind national security classifications, it is the perfect place to hide. (C.f. Oshkosh and AM General)

Forefront seems to be little more than a rendering at this stage, with the first of the Forefront concept prototypes set to take part in a number of exercises and trials in the months ahead to further refine the concept.

#4504. 9-foot-tall Game Boy Color plays all the classics

Published Nov 11, 2026 8:53 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever. Standing more than nine feet and weighing around 300 pounds, the Pokémon-yellow goliath requires a U-Haul to transport and took over 1,500 collective hours in a makerspace to create. And it isn’t just for show. The giant handheld plays real Game Boy games, thanks to a pixel-perfect display scaled up from the original and software written from scratch. The designers even fabricated an assortment of to-scale accessories, including game cartridges, a cable link, and AA batteries.

The console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons. It has also prompted plenty of older millennials, in person and online, to reminisce about simpler days. Build videos posted across social media have racked up hundreds of thousands of views. But for co-creator Paige Powell, a veteran prop designer and mechanical engineer, the giant Game Boy also represents something more special: a labor of love and a chance to inspire young girls to start building things themselves.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

“It [has] felt very weird to me in a very male-dominated world to build something behind the scenes and then give it to [a] guy who then takes credit,” Powell tells Popular Science. “I want people to see women making stuff!”

The giant GameBoy is the joint effort of Powell (@whats_paige_making on Instagram) and engineer Nick Alvarez (@nickbuildstuff on Instagram). Powell has a long track record of building props and sets for the YouTube channel Mega Builds and the immersive art company Meow Wolf. Alvarez, meanwhile, specializes in PCB (printed circuit board) design and spent seven years as a full-time engineering manager at an aerospace defense company.

The two crossed paths while working at the Davis makerspace, just west of Sacramento. Alvarez was building a large LED wall (the kind used for screens at sports arenas) and wanted to hook up Nintendo controllers so it could play games. Piggybacking off of that, Powell proposed taking the idea a step further: a giant playable Game Boy. From there, it only made sense to try and make the world’s largest. That sent them down a rabbit hole that would consume a sizable chunk of their lives (and finances) over the months to follow.

A quick bit of research revealed they weren’t the first one with this idea. Guinness World Records actually has an official entry for the Largest Game Boy Color, an accolade claimed in 2022 by a YouTuber named Jake Carlini. His version measured in at seven feet tall. But calling that one a real Game Boy is quite a stretch. It was really little more than a few pieces of vaguely detailed plywood. Alvarez and Powell realized there was an opportunity, not just to break the record, but to build something far more ambitious.

“It [the Carlini model] was just kind of [a] slapstick way of putting it together, and we were like, ‘dude, what is this?’ Alvarez says. ”We can do something actually amazing with our background and our skillset.”

From the outset, the duo gave themselves a set of constraints to build around. Their Game Boy had to be to scale to the original and functional as a game console. They also committed to making the screen pixel perfect to the 1998 original.

“Everything was built around the constraint of what the screen was going to be,” Powell says.

Fortunately, they had some help along the way. When they told Tim Keller, the head of the Davis makerspace, about the project, he agreed to let them set up shop and use the space’s CNC mills, 3D printers, laser cutters, and other equipment.

With goals set and tools secured, the pair then created a 3D model of their scaled-up Game Boy, starting with a smaller (though still shockingly large) 5.7-foot version. Powell quickly realized that the toughest part to fabricate wasn’t actually the console’s iconic front, but rather its geometrically odd-shaped back shell. The top of the backside starts out flat but then bulges out into a sloped shape toward the bottom where a person would hold it in their palm. The cartridge slot where the game slides into also juts out from the back, adding even more complexity

Once the 3D model was complete, Powell began building the physical body, made mostly of plywood shaped on the CNC machine, an automated manufacturing device that reads computer code and uses that to control cutting machines like mills, lathes, and lasers. CNC machines are indispensable tools in many makers’ arsenals. But a project like this requires adaptability. Partway through, Powell says, she realized the CNC machine wasn’t all that well suited to making square cuts, which meant the final product would need more hand carpentry than initially planned.

Meanwhile, Alvarez was hard at work perfecting the display and electronics under the hood (or, in this case, the shell). He built the screen from a series of HUB75 LED panels, the kind commonly used in large digital signs. The trick was getting his massive DIY display to scale up accurately from the original GameBoy’s 160-by-144 pixel screen. He also used a small microcontroller (essentially a tiny computer assigned to a specific task) to map all of the device’s buttons and switches.

When the giant Game Boy plays games, it’s running them on a specialized emulator rather than the physical game cartridge that gets slotted into the device. The emulator is a piece of software that imitates a Game Boy. Emulators are common these days and are what let hobbyists play old Nintendo games on smartphones.

The to-scale cartridges Powell and Alvarez fabricated are really more for show. That means, theoretically, their device can run any Game Boy game. Alvarez says he even built in a feature that cycles to a different game each time the power is switched on. So far, the pair have posted videos of the device playing Pokémon and Donkey Kong. Alvarez even watched The Odyssey on it.

Powell and Alvarez have shown off their creations at two events so far: Open Sauce in 2026 and the Bay Area Maker Fair in Vallejo, California. Getting the Game Boys there was a task in itself. The larger of the two (around 300 pounds) required a large U-Haul and four people just to load it. Once unloaded, they faced a more daunting challenge: the wrath of children. Drawn in by the device’s giant buttons, kids at the events let loose.

“Kids were coming up and karate-kicking them, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God, man,’” Powell says.

Alvarez concurs. “They were punching the crap out of the buttons.”

In a testament to its build quality, the giant Game Boy withstood the onslaught of toddler haymakers. Those who weren’t assailing the device were often absorbing an emotional gut punch of their own. Both in person and online, fans told Powell and Alvarez how the build brought back childhood memories. One commenter recalled how seeing it reminded them of a time at a school when a bully stole their beloved Game Boy. Decades later, he said, he’s still mad.

Looking ahead, Powell and Alvarez hope to find their creation a new home where it can be on display and accessible to the public. They’d like to recoup some of the money they’ve poured into it, but Powell also expressed some wariness of it winding up locked away in some buyer’s private collection. Ideally, she says, it would land in a museum of some kind, where it could inspire the next generation of budding makers.

#4503. Honda Investing $3 Billion to Build New Ohio Factory, Increase Hybrid Production in U.S.

The new plant will be capable of producing 240,000 vehicles a year, and multiple new models are currently under development.

Audi may have recently announced its first-ever U.S. production facility, but at least one Japanese automaker with a head start in that race doesn’t seem keen on giving up any places. On Monday, Honda announced it is investing $3 billion in a new central Ohio factory; the plant, which will produce up to 240,000 vehicles annually, is expected to be online by 2029.

Now, with nine production facilities across the U.S., Honda is no stranger to domestic production, but the new factory plan goes beyond merely adding production capacity. Instead, the company is targeting increased production of hybrid-electric vehicles and their accompanying drivetrain parts. The new plant will sit between Honda’s current East Liberty and Marysville Auto Plants, the carmaker said, and will focus on multiple vehicle types and powertrains, including hybrid and battery-electric vehicles. Honda said the plant will be one of the most advanced factories in the world, leveraging leading-edge automation, data-driven technologies and flexible production systems.

"As Honda approaches 50 years of building products close to our customers in America, we are making one of the most significant commitments in our history to position Honda for the next 50 years,” said Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor Co., Inc. “These investments strengthen America’s role as a cornerstone of Honda’s global future and reflect our confidence in our more than 30,000 Honda associates and the strength of American manufacturing. By expanding our comprehensive R&D and manufacturing capabilities, we will be better positioned to serve our customers and contribute to the economic vitality of the communities where we operate.”

Building another plant in Ohio was an easy choice for Honda. Honda’s U.S. supply base is nearby, and the automaker has a strong reputation among the region’s skilled workforce. The Japanese automaker has previously committed to launching 15 new Honda and Acura hybrid models globally by 2030; North America is the target for many of these models, which are currently in development at R&D facilities in California and Ohio. All told, Honda said the new plant will increase its annual U.S. production capacity to approximately 1.3 million vehicles a year.

The company’s Alabama Auto Plant will also receive new investment to expand engine production for a new V-6 hybrid engine; Honda will retool the engine production facility and one of the production lines to accommodate Passport SUV production. The Anna Engine Plant in Ohio will also be retooled, to produce a next-generation 4-cylinder Atkinson-cycle engine for future compact and midsize vehicles built in North America. Honda Transmission Plant-Ohio will be retooled for two next-generation Honda Hybrid systems in compact vehicles, while Honda Transmission Plant-Georgia will be retooled for next-generation hybrid systems in larger vehicles. All this retooling will account for a 250-percent increase in hybrid powertrain system capacity in Ohio.

“Honda's leadership could have chosen to build this plant anywhere in the world, but they chose Ohio because there are so many advantages to being here,” said Ohio governor Mike DeWine. “For almost half a century, Honda and Ohio have grown together, and generations of families have built their careers on Honda's manufacturing lines. Today's announcement isn't just an investment in a new facility—it's an investment in Ohio's people and Ohio's future.”
